newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU states must cut deficits structurally - Silguy.
newsitem.headline: EU states must cut deficits structurally - Silguy.

text.p: European Union member states must take structural steps in 1998 to reduce their public deficits durably and not make just one-off meaures, European Commissioner for monetary affairs, Yves Thibault de Silguy, said on Thursday.
"The meaures that must be taken for next year are structural measures, which will have a lasting effect," de Silguy told Reuters after a meeting in Paris.
A number of countries had taken "one-off" deficit reduction steps in 1997 but these would not help in 1998, he said.
"Many measures adopted in 1997 are what you call in English 'one-off' measures, they are not valid for 1998" de Silguy said.
Asked if this was how he looked on Italy's 1997 budget efforts, he replied: "notably, but not only Italy, other countries too".
De Silguy was speaking after meeting French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette for talks which he said had been devoted to a broad discussion of European affairs.

Forecasts issued by the European Commission on Wednesday notably showed Italy's public deficit coming in at 3.2 percent of gross domestic product this year and 3.9 percent of GDP in 1998, while the qualifying level for the euro is three percent of GDP. But the Commisison said it was still possible for Italy to rein its deficit in to three percent.

De Silguy defended the forecasts, which drew fire from Italy, stressing that they were only forecasts and the decision on who joined the euro single currency would be made next year once actual economic performance figures were available.
"These are forecasts, snapshots of the situation (at this moment in time). The forecasts for 1998 are forecasts based on a scenario if there were no policy change," he added.
"The Italians were at 6.7 percent for the deficit in 1996 and, according to our forecasts, they will be at 3.2 in 1997," he said. This was a cut "without precedent in Europe," he said.
"What is interesting about the forecasts, and it must be seen this way, is that there is very strong encouragement for Italy," he added.

Asked if he was worried by speculation in financial markets that forecasts -- showing other EU states producing precisely the three percent deficit level needed for the euro -- were politically influenced, de Silguy said absolutely not.
"The credibility of the figures is in the fact that they are not tampered with. I would not stand for any modifications," he said.
"Germany says 2.9 percent this year, we forecast three percent for Germany," he added.
